title: Article 8 and the proportionality structure
subtitle: The four-part qualification test — and the transferable tool hiding inside it
objectives: State the four-part test that qualifies (rather than defeats) a right under Article 8(2): in accordance with the law, legitimate aim, necessary in a democratic society, and proportionality
Explain the structured, four-stage proportionality test set out in Bank Mellat as a transferable analytical tool used well beyond Article 8
Apply the proportionality structure methodically to a new fact pattern, distinguishing a strong justification from a weak one on each stage rather than reaching for an instinctive answer

leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes that Article 8 proportionality in immigration cases is a structured judicial assessment, not a deferential review of the decision-maker's reasonableness

leadingAuthorities.citation: Bank Mellat v HM Treasury (No 2) [2013] UKSC 39
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the modern four-stage proportionality test used across public law and human rights adjudication
Distinguishes proportionality from Wednesbury unreasonableness and confirms proportionality's place in domestic rights adjudication

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Every qualified right in the Convention — Articles 8, 9, 10 and 11 — is qualified by structurally the same test. Learn it once, properly, here, and you reuse it for the rest of this module without relearning it from scratch each time.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the four stages by name already. The test pool here is weighted towards application: expect fact patterns where you have to work out which stage actually fails, not just recite the list.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and don't rush the statutory text in Part 2 — the whole lesson assumes you can reproduce the four-part structure without prompting before you get to the harder application work.

overview.hook: Almost every hard Article 8 problem question collapses into the same four questions, asked in the same order, every time. Learn that order properly here and you will not need to relearn it for Articles 9, 10 or 11 later in this module — or, in a different but closely related form, for judicial review. This lesson hands you the key. The rest of the module just changes which lock it opens.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. The structured proportionality test itself is settled Supreme Court doctrine (Bank Mellat, 2013) and is not a live currency point; this lesson's authorities are not expected to move.

parts.heading: Qualified rights aren't defeated — they're tested
parts.voice: master key — frames the whole lesson as one transferable tool the student will reuse across the module
body: Articles 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the Convention share a structure that is easy to miss on a first read because it's buried in the second paragraph of each article. Article 8(1) states the right — respect for private and family life, home and correspondence. Article 8(2) then says a public authority may interfere with that right, but only if the interference clears a specific, four-part hurdle.

This matters because a 'qualified right' is not a weak right. It is a right that shifts the argument: instead of asking 'was there an interference?' (usually easy to answer 'yes'), the real fight happens over whether the state can justify that interference. Article 8 problem questions are rarely won or lost on whether Article 8(1) is engaged — they are won or lost on the 8(2) justification.

Here is the four-part test, stated in the order the courts apply it. First: was the interference **in accordance with the law**? Second: did it pursue a **legitimate aim** listed in the article? Third: was it **necessary in a democratic society** — is there a pressing social need? Fourth: was it **proportionate** — even if all three of the above are satisfied, did the state go further than it needed to? Miss any one of these four and the interference is unlawful, however compelling the state's case looks on the others.

components.definition: A Convention right (Articles 8–11) that can lawfully be interfered with by the state, but only where the interference is in accordance with the law, pursues a legitimate aim, and is necessary and proportionate in a democratic society — contrasted with absolute rights (e.g. Article 3), which permit no justification at all, and limited rights (e.g. Article 5), which permit interference only on specific listed grounds without a free-standing proportionality inquiry.

interaction.prompt: Article 8 is a qualified right. Does that mean a state interference with private or family life is automatically lawful as long as some public interest is engaged?
options: No — the interference must still clear all four parts of the Article 8(2) test
Yes — 'qualified' means the right yields to any competing public interest
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. 'Qualified' describes the shape of the argument, not a weak right that folds at the first public-interest reason offered.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — a qualified right still requires the state to clear all four stages of the 8(2) test. Naming a public interest is only the second of four hurdles.

parts.heading: "In accordance with the law" and "legitimate aim" — the two gateway questions
parts.voice: structural — a reference part students will return to before exams
body: The first two stages of the test are usually the easiest for a well-prepared state to satisfy, but they are not rubber stamps, and examiners know it. 'In accordance with the law' requires more than a domestic legal power existing somewhere — the law must be accessible and its consequences foreseeable, so that a person can, with appropriate advice, regulate their conduct. A power that is vague, secret or applied unpredictably fails this stage even if a statute technically authorises it.

'Legitimate aim' asks whether the interference pursues one of the specific purposes listed in Article 8(2) itself: national security, public safety, the economic well-being of the country, the prevention of disorder or crime, the protection of health or morals, or the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. This is a closed list — the state cannot invent a new aim outside it, though in practice almost every real interference can be mapped onto one of these categories without much difficulty.

Students often rush past both stages to get to the more interesting 'proportionality' discussion. Resist that instinct. In a genuinely well-argued answer, a careless assumption that the first two stages are automatically satisfied is exactly the kind of gap an examiner is trained to notice.

components.citation: European Convention on Human Rights, Article 8
components.text: (1) Everyone has the right to respect for his private and family life, his home and his correspondence. (2) There shall be no interference by a public authority with the exercise of this right except such as is in accordance with the law and is necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security, public safety or the economic well-being of the country, for the prevention of disorder or crime, for the protection of health or morals, or for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.
elements: Pursuing a legitimate aim from the closed list in Article 8(2)

interaction.prompt: According to the text of Article 8(2) above, which of these is NOT one of the listed legitimate aims a state may rely on to justify an interference?
options: The economic well-being of the country
The prevention of disorder or crime
The promotion of national cultural identity
The protection of the rights and freedoms of others
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct — Article 8(2)'s list is closed, and 'promotion of national cultural identity' isn't on it. A state has to fit its justification into one of the six listed aims, not invent a seventh.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at the statutory text. The list in Article 8(2) is closed and specific; 'promotion of national cultural identity' does not appear in it, however plausible it sounds as a policy goal.

parts.heading: "Necessary in a democratic society" — the pressing social need
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the third stage through how courts have actually applied it
body: 'Necessary in a democratic society' does not mean 'indispensable', and it does not mean merely 'reasonable' or 'desirable' either. The Strasbourg and domestic case law settles on something in between: there must be a **pressing social need** for the interference, and the reasons given by the state must be **relevant and sufficient**.

This is where the state's justification has to do real work. It is not enough to assert that an interference serves a legitimate aim in the abstract — a court applying this stage asks whether, on the facts of this case, the need for that particular interference was actually pressing, given everything else going on. A generalised policy justification that hasn't grappled with the individual's circumstances tends to fail here.

R (Daly) v SSHD is the case that anchors this stage domestically, though its facts concern a related question — the intensity of scrutiny courts should apply. The House of Lords held that a blanket policy of excluding prisoners from their cells while their legal correspondence was examined went further than necessary to serve the (legitimate) aim of prison security; a case-by-case approach would have sufficed. Daly is really doing two jobs at once: it confirms proportionality is a distinct, more searching standard than ordinary Wednesbury review, and it shows 'necessary' failing not because the aim was illegitimate, but because a blanket approach couldn't show a pressing need for going that far in every case.

components.caseName: R (Daly) v Secretary of State for the Home Department
components.factsShort: A prisoner challenged a blanket Prison Service policy requiring prisoners to be excluded from their cells while officers examined legally privileged correspondence.
components.ratioShort: Proportionality requires asking whether a less intrusive measure could have achieved the aim; a blanket policy that goes further than necessary in every case fails that test even where the underlying aim is legitimate.

expanded.facts: Prison Service policy required prisoners to leave their cells while officers searched and read legally privileged correspondence, ostensibly to prevent intimidation of officers and to maintain security. Daly argued this breached his common law right to legal professional privilege and, separately, his Article 8 rights.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Steyn held that the intensity of review in a proportionality case is greater than under traditional Wednesbury grounds: the court must ask not merely whether the decision was within the range of reasonable responses, but whether the limitation of the right was no more than necessary to accomplish the objective, and whether a fair balance was struck.
expanded.significance: Daly is the leading domestic authority distinguishing proportionality from Wednesbury unreasonableness, and it is regularly cited outside Article 8 problem questions — including in judicial review answers — for that distinction alone.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario most likely to cause the 'necessary in a democratic society' stage to fail.
interaction.scenarioText: A local authority operates a rule requiring every visitor to a care home, without exception or individual assessment, to be searched and to surrender their phone for the full duration of every visit, applied identically regardless of the visitor's relationship to the resident or any individual risk factors.
tappableSpans: a local authority operates a rule
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the weak point. A blanket rule applied with no individual assessment struggles to show a pressing social need for going that far in every single case — exactly the flaw in the policy struck down in Daly.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the feature that stops the policy from being tailored to an actual risk. The problem isn't that a rule exists, or that it applies to visitors generally — it's the total absence of any case-by-case assessment.

parts.heading: The fourth stage: Bank Mellat's structured proportionality test
parts.voice: structural — sets out the transferable tool explicitly, naming it as such
body: Bank Mellat v HM Treasury (No 2) is the case to know for the modern, structured version of proportionality — and it did not arise on Article 8 facts at all. It concerned a Treasury direction effectively cutting an Iranian bank off from the UK financial system on national security grounds. The Supreme Court used the case to set out, clearly and in order, the four questions that now structure proportionality analysis across public law and human rights adjudication alike.

The four stages are: (1) is the objective sufficiently important to justify limiting a right? (2) is the measure rationally connected to that objective? (3) could a less intrusive measure have achieved the objective without unacceptably compromising it? (4) does a fair balance exist between the rights of the individual and the interests of the community, having regard to the severity and consequences of the interference?

Notice what this does to the fourth part of the Article 8(2) test: 'proportionality' is not one question but four, asked in a fixed sequence. A student who treats 'proportionality' as a single instinctive judgment — 'does this feel fair?' — is skipping most of the actual legal work. The examiner is looking for you to work through all four Bank Mellat stages, in order, and to identify which one the state's justification actually fails on.

This is also the lesson's cross-reference point: Public law's own lesson on irrationality and proportionality (in the judicial review context) teaches a closely related structure, because Bank Mellat's four stages are used there too. The two lessons do not duplicate each other — this one anchors the structure in Article 8 and the Convention-rights context; the Public law lesson applies the same underlying test to administrative decisions reviewed for Wednesbury-plus-proportionality grounds. If you've done that lesson already, treat this as confirmation, not new information; if you haven't, this is the fuller version.

components.label: The Bank Mellat four-stage proportionality test
points: Stage 1 — Is the objective sufficiently important to justify limiting a fundamental right?
Stage 2 — Is the measure rationally connected to that objective?
Stage 3 — Could a less intrusive measure have been used without unacceptably compromising the objective?
Stage 4 — Having regard to the severity of the measure's effects, has a fair balance been struck between the individual's rights and the interests of the community?

interaction.prompt: Put the Bank Mellat proportionality stages in the order a court applies them.
items: Is the objective sufficiently important to justify limiting a right?
Is the measure rationally connected to that objective?
Could a less intrusive measure have achieved the objective?
Does a fair balance exist between individual rights and the interests of the community?
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence. Each stage is a gate — a state that fails stage 1 or 2 never needs to reach the harder balancing exercise in stage 4, and a good answer says so explicitly rather than jumping straight to 'was it fair'.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — importance of the objective comes first, then rational connection, then the search for a less intrusive alternative, and only then the overall fair-balance question. Treat it as a sequence of gates, not four things to consider all at once.

parts.heading: Putting it together: Huang and structured deference
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the deference question before resolving it through Huang
body: Here's the question this final part resolves: when a court reviews a state decision on proportionality grounds, how much weight should it give to the original decision-maker's own judgment? Too little, and courts start re-making immigration and security policy themselves. Too much, and the proportionality test collapses back into Wednesbury deference — the very thing Daly said it wasn't.

Huang v SSHD answers this in the immigration context, but its reasoning is written generally enough to apply across Article 8. The House of Lords held that in an Article 8 appeal, the appellate authority's task is to decide for itself whether the interference — refusal of leave to remain, in Huang's case — is proportionate, not merely to review whether the original decision-maker's assessment was reasonable. The ultimate question of proportionality is one for the court or tribunal to answer directly.

That does not mean the original decision-maker's reasoning is irrelevant — weight can properly be given to it as part of the evidence going to stages 1 and 4 of Bank Mellat — but the court does not stop at asking 'was that a reasonable view to take?' It asks, itself, applying all four stages, whether the interference was actually proportionate. Huang is therefore the case that confirms this whole four-part structure is a genuine, structured judicial assessment — not a light-touch check on someone else's reasoning.

components.title: The full Article 8(2) test, assembled
components.description: How the four gateway questions and the four Bank Mellat proportionality stages fit together into a single structured test.

nodes.label: Was there an interference with an Article 8(1) right?
Was it in accordance with the law? (accessible, foreseeable legal basis)
Did it pursue a legitimate aim from the closed Article 8(2) list?
Was there a pressing social need — relevant and sufficient reasons?
Bank Mellat 1: is the objective sufficiently important?
Bank Mellat 2: is the measure rationally connected to it?
Bank Mellat 3: was a less intrusive measure available?
Bank Mellat 4: does a fair balance exist overall?
Interference is unlawful — fails at whichever stage

components.textAlternative: First confirm Article 8(1) is engaged. Then work through the Article 8(2) gateway questions in order: was the interference in accordance with the law, did it pursue a legitimate aim from the closed list, and was there a pressing social need for it. If all three are satisfied, move to the four Bank Mellat proportionality stages in sequence: is the objective sufficiently important, is the measure rationally connected to it, was a less intrusive measure available, and — only if the first three are passed — does a fair balance exist between the individual and the community. Failing at any stage makes the interference unlawful; the analysis does not require reaching every later stage once an earlier one has failed.

interaction.prompt: A local authority refuses a foreign national's application to remain in the UK on the basis of a general policy that treats any period of unemployment over six months as automatically disqualifying, applied to Amir without considering his specific circumstances: a British partner, two British children, and an active job offer starting in three weeks. Analyse whether the refusal is a proportionate interference with Amir's Article 8 rights.
factsToOrder: Amir has a British partner and two British children (established family life)
The policy applies an automatic six-month unemployment bar
No individual assessment of Amir's circumstances was carried out
Amir has an active job offer starting in three weeks

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether refusing Amir's application under an automatic, unindividuated policy is a proportionate interference with his Article 8(1) right to respect for family life.
modelAnswer.rule: Article 8(1) is engaged; interference must be in accordance with the law, pursue a legitimate aim, be necessary in a democratic society (a pressing social need shown by relevant and sufficient reasons), and satisfy the four Bank Mellat proportionality stages, applying the structured assessment confirmed in Huang rather than a light-touch review of the decision-maker's reasoning.
modelAnswer.application: Family life is plainly established (partner and children). The aim — effective immigration control — is legitimate. But a blanket six-month rule applied with no individual assessment struggles at the 'necessary' stage, echoing Daly, and at Bank Mellat stage 3: a less intrusive measure (an individualised assessment weighing the job offer and family ties) was plainly available and would not have compromised the immigration-control objective. Stage 4's fair balance also looks unfavourable to the state given the severity of the effect on two British children.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The refusal is likely a disproportionate interference: the state has a legitimate aim but has not shown it pursued it by the least intrusive means, and an automatic policy applied without any individual assessment is unlikely to survive the structured proportionality test.

testPool.prompt: State the four-part test that must be satisfied before a state interference with an Article 8(1) right is lawful under Article 8(2).
acceptableAnswers: in accordance with the law, legitimate aim, necessary in a democratic society, proportionate
lawful basis, legitimate aim, necessity, proportionality
testPool.modelAnswer: The interference must be (1) in accordance with the law, (2) in pursuit of a legitimate aim listed in Article 8(2), (3) necessary in a democratic society (a pressing social need), and (4) proportionate.

testPool.prompt: Which case is the leading domestic authority for the proposition that proportionality is a more intensive standard of review than Wednesbury unreasonableness?
options: R (Daly) v SSHD
R v Stone and Dobinson

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a legitimate aim listed in Article 8(2)?
options: National security
Prevention of disorder or crime
Promotion of a state's international reputation
Protection of health or morals
testPool.trapExplanation: Article 8(2)'s list of legitimate aims is closed and specific: national security, public safety, economic well-being, prevention of disorder or crime, protection of health or morals, and protection of the rights and freedoms of others. 'Promotion of a state's international reputation' is not on it, however plausible it might sound as a policy justification.

testPool.prompt: Put the four Bank Mellat proportionality stages in the order a court applies them.
items: Is the measure rationally connected to the objective?
Was a less intrusive measure available?
Does a fair balance exist overall?

testPool.prompt: "In accordance with the law" requires more than a domestic legal power existing. What additional quality must the law have?
options: It must be accessible and its consequences reasonably foreseeable
It must have been enacted within the last five years
It must have been approved by referendum

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from R (Daly) v SSHD, highlight the sentence that states the ratio on the standard of review.
testPool.passage: The Prison Service's blanket policy required every prisoner to be excluded from their cell while privileged correspondence was examined. The intensity of review in a case involving a fundamental right is greater than under traditional Wednesbury grounds; the question is not merely whether the decision fell within a range of reasonable responses, but whether the limitation of the right was no more than was necessary to accomplish the objective. Applying that standard, the blanket policy went further than was necessary in every case.
testPool.ratioSentence: The intensity of review in a case involving a fundamental right is greater than under traditional Wednesbury grounds; the question is not merely whether the decision fell within a range of reasonable responses, but whether the limitation of the right was no more than was necessary to accomplish the objective.

testPool.prompt: What does Huang v SSHD add to the proportionality test beyond the four Bank Mellat stages?
options: It confirms that the court or tribunal must decide proportionality for itself, rather than merely reviewing whether the original decision-maker's view was reasonable
It removes the need to show a legitimate aim in immigration cases
It confirms that proportionality only applies to Article 8, not to other qualified rights
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers misdescribe Huang as narrowing the test (removing the legitimate aim requirement) or confining it to one article. Huang's real contribution is about the standard of review: the court decides proportionality itself rather than deferring to whether the original decision was 'reasonable'.

testPool.prompt: A council introduces CCTV monitoring inside all social housing communal stairwells, with footage retained indefinitely and accessible to all housing officers regardless of role. A resident challenges this under Article 8. At which Bank Mellat stage is this policy most vulnerable?
options: Stage 3 — a less intrusive measure (time-limited retention, restricted access) was plainly available without compromising the security objective
Stage 1 — the objective of tenant safety is not sufficiently important
Stage 2 — CCTV is not rationally connected to safety
testPool.explanation: Tenant safety is a legitimate and important objective, and CCTV is rationally connected to it, so stages 1 and 2 are likely satisfied. The real weakness is stage 3: indefinite retention and unrestricted internal access go further than necessary when a more tailored policy would serve the same aim.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact most likely to cause this measure to fail the 'necessary in a democratic society' stage.
testPool.scenarioText: A prison introduces a policy that all family visits, for every prisoner regardless of category or history, must take place through a glass screen with no physical contact permitted, applied uniformly with no provision for review or exception.
tappableSpans: for every prisoner regardless of category or history
must take place through a glass screen
no provision for review or exception
testPool.correctSpan: no provision for review or exception
testPool.explanation: The absence of any mechanism to review or except individual cases is what prevents the state showing a pressing social need for going this far with every prisoner, regardless of their actual risk profile.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more closely tracks the reasoning in Daly, rather than a case that would likely satisfy the proportionality test?
testPool.scenarioA: A prison searches an individual prisoner's cell following specific intelligence that he is concealing a weapon, in his absence, following an internal review of the evidence.
testPool.scenarioB: A prison requires every prisoner to be excluded from their cell during any legal correspondence review, applied identically regardless of any individual risk assessment.
testPool.explanation: B mirrors Daly precisely: a blanket rule applied without individual assessment, going further than necessary in every case. A, by contrast, is individually targeted and evidence-based — exactly the kind of tailored measure that tends to survive the 'necessary' and 'less intrusive alternative' stages.

testPool.prompt: In an Article 8 appeal, should the tribunal ask whether the original refusal decision was a 'reasonable' one to take, or decide proportionality for itself?
options: Decide proportionality for itself, per Huang
Ask only whether the original decision was reasonable

testPool.prompt: Border officials seize and copy the entire contents of a returning traveller's phone at random, as part of an unpublicised general practice with no case-specific suspicion, retaining the data indefinitely. Analyse the Article 8 proportionality of this practice.
factsToOrder: There is no case-specific suspicion (random selection)
The entire contents of the phone are copied (broad scope)
Data is retained indefinitely (no time limit)

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether an unpublicised, suspicionless, indefinite phone-data seizure practice is a lawful interference with Article 8.
modelAnswer.rule: The interference must be in accordance with the law (accessible and foreseeable), pursue a legitimate aim, be necessary (a pressing social need), and satisfy the four Bank Mellat proportionality stages.
modelAnswer.application: An unpublicised practice is unlikely to be 'in accordance with the law' at all, since it fails the foreseeability requirement before proportionality is even reached. Even assuming that hurdle were cleared, the lack of case-specific suspicion, the breadth of data copied, and indefinite retention all point to a failure at Bank Mellat stage 3 — a more targeted, time-limited practice tied to actual suspicion would achieve the border-security objective with far less intrusion.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The practice is very likely unlawful, arguably failing at the 'in accordance with the law' gateway stage and, in any event, failing the proportionality test on scope and retention.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that the proportionality test always requires the state to adopt the single least intrusive measure imaginable, however marginal the difference in effectiveness?
sliderLabels: Not required — 'less intrusive' is compared against effectiveness, not chosen in isolation
testPool.correctPosition: Not required — 'less intrusive' is compared against effectiveness, not chosen in isolation
testPool.explanation: Bank Mellat stage 3 asks whether a less intrusive measure could have achieved the objective without unacceptably compromising it — it is a comparative, not absolute, question. A marginally less intrusive measure that meaningfully undermines the objective does not have to be preferred.

testPool.prompt: Which case supplies the modern, structured four-stage version of the proportionality test used across public law and human rights adjudication, and did not itself arise on Article 8 facts?
options: Bank Mellat v HM Treasury (No 2)
Huang v SSHD
R (Daly) v SSHD
testPool.explanation: Bank Mellat arose from a Treasury direction on national security grounds against an Iranian bank, not from Article 8 facts — but its four-stage structure is now the standard proportionality test applied across public law and Convention-rights cases alike, including Article 8.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating 'proportionality' as one holistic gut-check rather than four sequential gates. A strong answer identifies exactly which Bank Mellat stage the state's justification fails on — not just that it 'feels' disproportionate.
